methodological_questions: confounding by score effects and opponent quality
label error in defensive scheme classification

historical_evidence.finding: Only 2 of 30 stars (7%) showed a stable (75% or more same top suppressor) top sequential suppressor across seasons. Negative teammate pair effects were found but not seasonally stable.
Among 653 eligible players, correlation between a defender's fingerprint displacement (D_A) and opponent PPP allowed was +0.020, i.e., essentially zero. High-D_A players often allowed more PPP.

Within-game and cross-game defensive scheme changes were high (~61-68%), but near-uniform transition matrices indicated that the reverse-inferred labels could not separate real defensive adjustment from offensive execution changes. The question was deemed unanswerable with that labeling approach.

Apparent adaptation effects disappeared when design flaws (label error, selection bias, mechanical floor) were accounted for. The asymmetry, confidence and carryover tests did not support a real defensive coverage response.
Play-type label backfill verification failed: PNR share outside expected range, PULL_UP shares near 0-2% for many teams in 2024-25, indicating severe label error in derived play-type data.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Inferring defensive scheme changes from opponent PPP outcomes to test within-game and cross-game adaptation.
failed_approaches.why: Label noise and inability to distinguish defensive action from offensive execution changes (LIM:label_or_classification_error).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Measuring season-to-season stability of a star's top sequential suppressor as a defensive trait.
failed_approaches.why: Adequately powered null result: only 7% of stars met the stability rule (B_powered_null).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Using defensive reorganization fingerprint (D_A) to predict opponent PPP suppression.
failed_approaches.why: No correlation (corr=+0.020) despite adequate sample; high-D_A players often allowed more PPP (B_powered_null).

evidence_establishes: Previously tested defensive traits (top suppressor stability, reorganizer-PPP link) showed near-zero effect or null results.
Play-type labels derived from outcome data suffer from systematic errors, making any analysis relying on them unreliable.
Attempts to infer defensive adjustments from PPP changes were confounded by offensive execution, leading to untestable claims.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 scoring change is a reliable team trait, as no study directly measured this metric.
The true variance and potential statistical power for an H2-H1 change ICC using 120 team-seasons.
That all defensive traits are inherently unreliable; the failure of specific traits does not guarantee failure for all.
own_inferences: The H2-H1 opponent points difference is a noisy metric influenced by score effects, opponent adjustments, fatigue, and game script, likely yielding a low true team-level ICC.
Even if a modest ICC exists (e.g., 0.15), 120 team-seasons may provide only ~4 repeated observations per team, resulting in wide confidence intervals and low power to exclude a near-zero ICC.
The prior null results on defensive trait stability raise the bar for what constitutes a worthwhile test without stronger design controls.
uncertainties: True effect size and variance of team-level H2-H1 opponent change after adjusting for confounders.
Optimal way to control for opponent offensive strength (e.g., full-season rating vs. game-by-game).
Whether within-season split-half reliability could be higher and more detectable than cross-season stability.

historical_effect.explanation: The failure of top suppressor stability (SF-APPA-058) and the null reorganizer-PPP result (SF-PAP-030) strongly suggest that defensive traits are fragile and hard to detect. This shifts the prior probability of a successful test downward and, combined with the known label issues, makes a straightforward study unlikely to yield a reliable answer, reinforcing a do_not_proceed decision.

blocking_constraints.text: 120 team-seasons (30 teams x 4 seasons) provides only 4 repeated measures per team for cross-season reliability; expected ICC for a noisy metric may be small, giving low power to distinguish from zero.
H2-H1 opponent points difference has high game-to-game variance from score effects, opponent lineups, and game script; the resulting team-season average may have limited reliability.
Half-time score differential, opponent offensive quality, back-to-back fatigue, and lineup changes could drive H2-H1 changes independently of any stable defensive trait.

prior_work.summary: Earlier work tested two different defensive trait hypotheses—season stability of top suppressors and defensive reorganization impact on PPP—both returned null or untestable results. Play-type label errors were a recurring confound. No study directly examined H2-H1 opponent change as a team trait, but the failures of related defensive reliability tests suggest a low prior probability of success.

risks.text: With only 120 team-seasons (30 teams x 4 seasons), the effective sample for cross-season ICC is approximately 30 independent units with 4 repeats, which may be insufficient to detect a small to moderate ICC.
H2-H1 scoring change is a difference score with inherently lower reliability; team-level aggregates may still contain substantial noise.
Score effects (teams ahead at half may alter strategy), opponent quality differences between seasons, and in-game adjustments unrelated to a stable team trait could introduce bias.
If the effect is to be attributed to specific defensive play types or schemes, the known play-type label inaccuracies (SF-APPA-030) would contaminate the measurement.
Selecting teams with extreme H2-H1 changes for post-hoc analysis could inflate apparent reliability due to regression to the mean.

design.estimand: Intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) of team-season average opponent points per 100 possessions difference (H2 minus H1), adjusted for opponent offensive rating and game-level confounders, across the 2022-23 through 2025-26 seasons.
design.unit: Team-season (30 teams × 4 seasons = 120 observations, grouped by team).
design.sample: All regular-season games from 2022-23 through 2025-26; exclude playoff games to maintain consistent game-script dynamics.
design.power: Assuming a true ICC of 0.20 and 4 repeats per team, power to reject ICC=0 at alpha=0.05 with 30 teams is approximately 0.40 (based on Fisher transformation approximation). To reach 80% power, >60 teams would be required, or a within-season split-half design (e.g., odd/even games) yielding ~40 pseudo-repeats could be explored instead.
design.controls: 1) Half-time score differential (quadratic if needed) to adjust for score effects; 2) Opponent's full-season offensive rating (or game-level offensive rating) as a fixed effect; 3) Indicator for home/away and back-to-back; 4) Season fixed effect to absorb league-wide trend.
design.falsification: Negative control: compute ICC using same approach but on a placebo outcome (e.g., opponent first-half points vs. opponent second-half points of previous game) which should show near-zero reliability. Also test split-half reliability within a single season (game 1-41 vs. 42-82) to see if the trait is stable only within season but not across.
design.multiplicity: One primary test: ICC point estimate with 95% CI; no multiple comparisons across subgroups.
design.decision_rule: Proceed to claim trait is reliable only if the lower 95% confidence bound of the ICC exceeds 0.10 after adjustment for multiple testing (if any secondary analyses are run). Otherwise, report null.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game files snapshot as of 2026-10-06; play-by-play to derive opponent points per possession; team-level info from box-score summaries.

separating defensive skill from opponent and game context

- Team trait: Something that is a stable characteristic of a team, i.e., repeatable across games, across seasons, or within a season.
- Reliability: In a psychometric or statistical sense, whether this effect is consistent (reliable) across different games/contexts for the same team.
